lessons.title: Making Connections
lessons.originalProblem: RI.K.3 is connecting two individuals/events/ideas in a text; this lesson quietly drifts into cause-and-effect only. The teach example (sun is hot, plants need sun) and the caterpillar example mix loose 'relatedness' with causation, so the through-line of what 'connection' means is a little muddy for a 5-year-old.

steps.ttsScript: In fact books, two pieces of information can go together, like puzzle pieces that fit!
Making a connection means finding how two facts are about the same thing.
Let's learn to link facts together!
Two facts connect when they belong to the same thing.
Like this: A frog has long back legs. A frog can jump very far. Both facts are about the frog, so they link together!
Linking two facts helps us understand the whole picture!
Listen to two facts about a bird. Let's find how they link!
Fact one: An owl has big round eyes.
steps.displayText: An owl has big round eyes.

steps.ttsScript: Fact two: An owl hunts at night.
How do they link? Both facts are about the owl! Big eyes and hunting at night go together.
Here is a trick to find a connection. Ask one tiny question!
Ask: are these two facts about the same thing?
If yes, the two facts connect!
You're a connection master!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Now you try, detective! Here are two facts. A bee has tiny wings. A bee can fly from flower to flower. What do both facts tell us about?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! Both facts are about the bee. You linked them together all by yourself!
interactive.wrongScript: So close! Listen again. Both facts name the same little buzzy animal. Try again!

steps.ttsScript: Amazing work! You know how to link two facts like a pro!
steps.displayText: You link facts like a pro

steps.ttsScript: Let's practice finding connections. Let's go!

lessons.title: Parts of a Book
lessons.originalProblem: Only 1 practice MCQ (vs. 5 in the siblings), so the kid gets almost no independent reps after instruction; the lesson also slightly overstuffs the teach slide with four parts at once before any practice.

steps.ttsScript: Did you know a book has special parts, just like your body does?
Today we'll meet the front cover, the back cover, and the title page.
Let's see what each one does!
The front cover is the very first thing you see. It shows the title and a picture.

displayParts.text: Front cover: first thing you see

steps.ttsScript: Flip the book over to the other side. That's the back cover.
Open the book and look inside. The first page is the title page.
The title page names the book and tells who made it.
Let's try one together! Here is a brand-new book.
On the front you see a big spider and the words All About Bugs.
What part shows the picture and the name? The front cover!
Where do we find who made it? The title page inside!
You spotted both parts. You're a book expert!
Here's a trick. The cover is on the outside, and the title page is on the inside.
Outside greets you, inside tells who made it!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Now you try, detective! Sam opened his book all the way to the inside. The first page named the book and showed who wrote it. What part did Sam find?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! The title page! It's inside and tells who made the book. You found it all by yourself!
interactive.wrongScript: So close! Sam was looking inside the book at who made it. Try again!

steps.ttsScript: Great work learning the parts of a book!
Your turn now. Let's spot some book parts!

lessons.title: Reasons and Support
lessons.originalProblem: the 'Your Turn' Leo item is really find-a-detail, not identify-a-reason-that-supports-a-point, so it drifts from the actual standard

steps.ttsScript: An author makes a point. That is something they want us to believe.
Then they give reasons. Reasons tell us why the point is true!
Today we find the reasons that hold up a point. Let's go!
Here is a point: Recess is the best part of school.
Why? Because you get to run. Because you play with friends. Those are reasons!
Each reason supports the point. They tell us why recess is best!
Let's try one together! Here is a point an author makes.
Cats are easy pets. They clean themselves. They sleep a lot. They are quiet!
steps.displayText: They clean themselves. They sleep a lot. They are quiet!

steps.ttsScript: What is one reason cats are easy pets? They clean themselves!
That reason supports the point. It tells us why cats are easy. You found it!
First find the point. Then ask: why is that true?
The answer to why is the reason that supports the point!
Now you are a reason detective!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Now you try! An author makes this point: Bees are helpful. Here is what the author writes. Bees are helpful. They make sweet honey. They help flowers grow. Which one is a reason that bees are helpful?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! Making honey is a reason that supports the point that bees are helpful!
interactive.wrongScript: Not quite! Stripes and flying are just details. Which one tells why bees are HELPFUL? Try again!

steps.ttsScript: Wonderful! You can find the reasons that support a point!
Now let's practice finding reasons on your own. You've got this!

lessons.title: Vowel Sounds
lessons.originalProblem: Tries to teach too much for one K lesson — short vs long vowels AND Magic E AND 'every word needs a vowel' — yet the interactive only checks identifying a vowel in 'fish', so the harder concepts go unpracticed and may overwhelm

steps.ttsScript: Today we learn that vowels can make two different sounds!
A short sound, that's quick and snappy.
And a long sound, where the vowel says its own name!
Listen to the short A sound. Aaa.
You hear it in the word cat. Cat.
The short sound is quick. Aaa. Cat!
Now listen to the long A sound. Aaay.
You hear it in the word cake. Cake.
The long sound says its name! A! Cake!
Let's try one together. Listen to this word.
Here is the word: pin. Pin.
Does it have a short sound or a long sound? Short! Pin.
Now the word pine. Pine. That long I says its name! Pine!
Here is a trick to remember.
If the vowel says its own name, it's the long sound!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Now you try! Listen closely. Here is the word: bed. Bed. Does bed have a short sound or a long sound?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! Bed has a short E sound. It's quick and snappy, not saying its name!
interactive.wrongScript: So close! Listen again. Bed. Does the vowel say its name, or is it quick? Try again!

steps.ttsScript: You can hear short and long sounds! That's a big deal!
Let's practice listening for vowel sounds. Ready? Let's go!

lessons.title: Using New Words
lessons.originalProblem: the Your Turn tests synonym/comprehension (which word means big) rather than the taught skill of USING a new word in a sentence

steps.ttsScript: You learn new words all the time! But the best part is using them!
When you put a new word into your own sentence, that word becomes yours!
Let's practice using new words in sentences!
When you learn a new word, build a sentence around it right away!
Say you learn the word 'gigantic.' You could say: The blue whale is gigantic!
See how the word fit right into the sentence? That is using a new word!
Let's try one together! Here's a new word: 'cozy.' It means warm and snug.
Now let's use it in a sentence. Which one sounds right? My bed is cozy!
You just used 'cozy' in your very own sentence! You're a vocabulary superstar!
Here's a trick. To use a new word, ask: what could I say about it?
Then start your sentence and slide the new word right inside!
One little sentence, and that word is yours forever!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Now you try! Here's a brand-new word: 'joyful.' It means very happy. Which sentence uses the word joyful the right way?

choices: We were joyful at the party!
I drank a glass of joyful.
interactive.correct: We were joyful at the party!
interactive.correctScript: Yes! 'We were joyful at the party!' You used the new word in a sentence all by yourself!
interactive.wrongScript: So close! Joyful means very happy. Find the sentence where it fits just right. Try again!

steps.ttsScript: You're putting new words into your very own sentences!
Let's practice using new words the right way. Let's go!

lessons.title: Retelling Stories
lessons.originalProblem: the Your Turn only asks to identify the problem (the middle), not to retell/sequence B-M-E, which is the real skill

steps.ttsScript: Retelling means telling a story in your own words.
You keep the most important parts.
And you tell them in order.
Every story has three big parts, in order.
First, the beginning. Who is in it and what is happening?
Next, the middle. What is the problem or big event?
Last, the end. How does it all work out?
Let's try one together. Listen to this story.
Tom wanted to win the race. His shoe came untied! He tied it fast and crossed the finish line.
steps.displayText: Tom wanted to win the race. His shoe came untied! He tied it and finished.

steps.ttsScript: What happened at the beginning? Tom wanted to win!
What happened in the middle? His shoe came untied!
And the end? He tied it and finished! You retold all three parts!
Here is a trick. Use order words.
Say first, then next, then last.
Now you are ready to practice retelling!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Now you retell! Here's a new story. Lily wanted to bake muffins. She found her bowl was empty with no flour! So she borrowed some from her neighbor and baked them. Match each event to its part of the story.

interactive.prompt: Match each event to its part
interactive.correctScript: You retold the whole story in order! Beginning, she wanted muffins. Middle, no flour. End, she borrowed some and baked!
interactive.wrongScript: Not quite. Think about what happened first, next, and last. Try again!

lessons.title: Words That Show Feelings
lessons.originalProblem: the Your Turn answer 'Tears' is a noun/thing, not the kind of vivid feeling-word the lesson just modeled, so the item undercuts the teaching

steps.ttsScript: Writers pick special words to make us feel something.
Some words let us hear, see, or touch a story in our mind.
Let us go find some feeling words!
Today we learn words that tell us how a character feels.
Words like happy, excited, or joyful show us good feelings.
Words like sad, angry, or scared show us harder feelings.
These feeling words help us understand the story.
Watch how one word changes everything. Here is a plain sentence: She walked to the door.
Now I swap in a feeling word. She stomped to the door. Stomped makes me feel she is angry! Same girl, but one word shows how she feels inside.
Let's try one together. Listen to this sentence.
The puppy bounced across the yard.
steps.displayText: The puppy bounced across the yard.

steps.ttsScript: Which word shows the puppy feels happy? Bounced!
Bounced makes us feel how excited and happy that puppy is!
Here is a helpful trick.
When you read a feeling word, stop and feel it for a moment.
Now you are ready to find feeling words on your own!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Your turn! Read this sentence. The hungry boy gobbled his lunch. Which word shows how the boy feels?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! Gobbled! That word lets us feel just how hungry the boy was!
interactive.wrongScript: So close! Which word shows how he ate? Listen again and try once more!

steps.ttsScript: You are a feeling-word finder now! Let's practice.
Read each sentence and find the word that makes you feel it.

lessons.title: Parts of a Fact Book
lessons.originalProblem: teaches three text features but only tests one (TOC); no worked example, so it names parts more than it models using them to find info

steps.ttsScript: Fact books have special parts that help you find facts fast.
Today we meet three helpers: contents, headings, and labels.
Each one helps you find something different. Let us see how!
The table of contents is up front. It lists chapters and their page numbers.
A heading is the big words at the top. It tells what the page is about.
A label is a little word that points to a part of a picture.
Let's try one together! You want to find facts about frogs.
Which part shows you what page frogs start on? The contents!

displayParts.text: What page do frogs start on?

steps.ttsScript: Now you are on the frog page. Which part names the frog's legs? The label!
You used the parts to find facts. Nice work!
Here is a handy trick to remember.
Ask what you need! A page number? Use contents. A picture part? Use a label.
Pick the right helper, and you will find any fact!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: You've got it - now you try! Match each book part to the job it does for you.

interactive.prompt: Match each part to its job
interactive.correctScript: You matched them all! Contents shows pages, a heading tells the topic, and a label names a picture part!
interactive.wrongScript: Not quite - think about what each part helps you find. Try again!

steps.ttsScript: Your turn! Let's use book parts to find facts.
Remember your three helpers and you will do great!

lessons.title: Word Beginnings and Endings
lessons.originalProblem: The tip slide abruptly switches to a third affix (-ed) that was never taught in the teach slides and isn't practiced, so it crams in an unmodeled concept; the lesson teaches un-/-er but the tip muddies the focus

steps.ttsScript: Little word parts can change what a word means.
They stick on the beginning or the end.
Let us meet a few!
The ending E R can mean one who does.
Teacher? One who teaches!
Runner? One who runs!
The beginning U N means not.
Unhappy? Not happy!
Unlock? Not locked!
Let us try one together. Here is a word.
Here is the word: painter.
What is the word part on the end? E R!
So what does painter mean? One who paints!
Here is a trick for these little parts.
Find the part, then say what it means.
steps.displayText: Find the part, say its meaning

steps.ttsScript: U N at the front means not. E R at the end means one who does.

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Your turn! Remember, UN means not. What does the word unzip mean?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! Not zipped! UN at the front means not, so you cracked it!
interactive.wrongScript: So close! UN means not. So what does unzip mean? Try again!

lessons.title: Using Big Words
lessons.originalProblem: The example beat is filler ('use new words') rather than a modeled application, leaving the teaching a bit abstract

steps.ttsScript: Great readers and writers pick the just-right word.
The right word makes a sentence clear!
Let us practice.
When you read a sentence with a blank, think about what fits.
The kids were hungry. They ate a blank.
steps.displayText: The kids were hungry. They ate a ___.

steps.ttsScript: A banquet? Yes! A symphony? No!
Let's try one together. Here is a sentence with a blank.
The storm was loud. The thunder was very blank.
Which word fits? Noisy? Yes!
Why not silent? Silent means no sound at all!
So the thunder was very noisy. You picked the just-right word!
Here is a helpful trick.
Ask, does this word fit the meaning of my sentence?
Now you are ready to use big words!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Your turn! Listen to this sentence. The little puppy was so small. It was very... which word best fits the blank?

interactive.prompt: Puppy was small. It was very ___.
interactive.correctScript: Yes! Tiny! Tiny means very small, so it fits the puppy perfectly!
interactive.wrongScript: So close! The puppy was small. Which word means small? Try again!

steps.ttsScript: Your turn! Let's practice picking the just-right word.
Remember, the right word fits the meaning.

lessons.title: The Shape of a Story
lessons.originalProblem: The teaching is thin and abstract — it tells kids what each part does but never models it on an actual story before the interactive, so there's no worked example bridging the explanation to the 'Your Turn'; a child weak on this would jump from definitions straight to application

steps.ttsScript: Every story has a shape. A beginning, middle, and end.
The shape helps us follow along.
Let us look at each part.
The beginning introduces us. Who is the story about? Where are they?
It sets up the whole story.
The middle is where most of the action happens.
There is usually a problem or a big event.
The end wraps things up. How did it all turn out?
Let us map a real story together. Here it is.
Sam woke up on the farm. His goat got loose and ran off! Sam chased it and brought it home.
steps.displayText: Sam's goat got loose. Sam brought it home.

steps.ttsScript: How does it start? Sam wakes up on the farm. That is the beginning!
What is the problem? The goat got loose! That is the middle.
How does it finish? Sam brings the goat home. That is the end. You mapped the whole shape!
Here is a helpful trick.
As you read, ask: am I in the beginning, middle, or end?
Now you are ready to see the shape of a story!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Your turn, story detective! Listen to this little story. Lily the squirrel woke up hungry and spotted a big acorn under an oak tree. Suddenly, a black crow swooped down and wanted the acorn too! Lily chattered loudly and held on tight, until the crow flew away and she buried her acorn safely. The crow swooping down for the acorn is the problem. What part of the story is that?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! The middle! That is where the problem and the action happen!
interactive.wrongScript: Not quite! The problem comes after the story sets up who and where. Which part is that? Try again!

lessons.title: Finding the Big Idea
lessons.originalProblem: The Your Turn distractors are weak: 'Dogs' vs 'Playing fetch'/'Training tricks' lets a kid pick the answer just by spotting the most-repeated noun rather than by synthesizing the big idea, so it under-tests the skill it just taught

steps.ttsScript: Longer fact texts have lots of little ideas.
But one big idea holds them all together.
That big idea is called the main topic.
Each paragraph focuses on a smaller part of the big idea.
One detail tells what something is.
Another detail tells why it matters.
All the details point back to the main topic.
Let's try one together. Here is a short text about honey bees.
Bees buzz from flower to flower. They turn nectar into sweet honey.
steps.displayText: Bees gather nectar and make honey.

steps.ttsScript: Is the big idea buzzing, or honey bees?
Honey bees! Buzzing is just one little detail. Every sentence is about the bees.
Here is a helpful trick.
Don't just pick the word you hear most. Ask: what is this text mostly about?
The big idea covers every sentence, not just one.

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Listen closely. 'Penguins waddle across the ice on their short legs. They dive into the cold sea to catch fish. Their thick feathers keep them warm in the freezing cold.' Which sentence tells the BIG idea of the whole text?

choices: Penguins are built for life in the icy cold.
Penguins dive into the sea to catch fish.
Penguins have short legs for waddling.
interactive.correct: Penguins are built for life in the icy cold.
interactive.correctScript: Yes! That's the big idea! The legs, the diving, and the warm feathers all connect to living in the icy cold.
interactive.wrongScript: That's a real detail, but it's only one sentence. Which choice covers the WHOLE text? Try again!

steps.ttsScript: You're ready! Time to practice finding the big idea on your own.
Remember, the big idea ties every sentence together.

lessons.title: How Authors Back Up Their Points
lessons.originalProblem: the Your Turn asks for the main point, not the reasons that support it, so the guided practice tests main-idea rather than RI.2.8's actual skill

steps.ttsScript: When an author makes a point, they give reasons.
The reasons back up the point.
Spotting reasons makes you a strong reader!
Point: you should drink water every day.
Why? Reason one: it helps your body work.
Reason two: it stops you from feeling tired.
Two reasons hold up the point!
Let's try one together. Here's an author's point.
steps.displayText: Recess is the best part of school.

steps.ttsScript: The author says we run, we play, and we make friends.
Which reason backs up the point? We make friends!
That reason backs up the point. You found it!
Here is a helpful trick.
Watch for words like because, since, and for example. Those signal reasons!
After those words comes a reason!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Listen closely. 'Dogs make great pets. They keep you safe because they bark at strangers. They also play fetch and love long walks.' Which reason backs up the point that dogs make great pets?

interactive.prompt: Which reason backs up the point?
interactive.correctScript: Yes! They bark at strangers is a reason that backs up the point! You spotted the proof!
interactive.wrongScript: That's the point, not a reason. Listen again — what reason does the author give? Try again!

steps.ttsScript: Your turn! Now you'll find the reasons authors give.
Remember to listen for because and since.

lessons.title: Comparing Two Fact Books
lessons.originalProblem: the Your Turn compares two kids talking about pets rather than two texts on a topic, and only asks for the similarity, never the contrast, so it doesn't model comparing two books

steps.ttsScript: Two fact books can be about the very same topic.
But each author picks different details to share.
Reading both gives you a bigger picture.
First, find what both books agree on. That is the same.
Then, find what only one book says. That is different.
Comparing means spotting both at once!
Let's try one together. Two books are about frogs.
Book One says: Frogs hop. They eat bugs. Book Two says: Frogs hop. They lay eggs in water.
steps.displayText: Book 1: hop, eat bugs. Book 2: hop, lay eggs.

steps.ttsScript: What do both books say? Frogs hop!
What is only in Book Two? They lay eggs!
You found the same point and the different one. Great comparing!
Here is a helpful trick.
Make a two-column chart. Same on one side, different on the other.
Now you are ready to compare two fact books!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Two fact books are about bees. Book One says bees buzz and bees make honey. Book Two says bees buzz and bees live in a hive. Match each idea to where it belongs!

interactive.prompt: Match each idea to where it belongs
interactive.correctScript: You did it! Both books say bees buzz, but only Book One says honey and only Book Two says hive. You compared and contrasted two books!
interactive.wrongScript: Not quite. Buzz is in both books. Honey is only in Book One, hive is only in Book Two. Try again!

steps.ttsScript: Your turn to compare two fact books on your own!
Remember: find the same point, then the different one.

lessons.title: Reading Facts All Year
lessons.originalProblem: by nature it can't truly 'teach' year-long reading proficiency, so it leans motivational over skill-building

steps.ttsScript: Informational books are full of true facts.
Good readers find those facts right in the words.
First, read the sentence slowly.
Then ask: what fact does it tell me?
The answer is hiding right in the text.
A question asks who, what, or where.
Look back and point to the matching words.
Let's try one together. Here's a short fact.
The sun is a huge star. It gives us light and heat.
steps.displayText: The sun is a huge star. It gives us light and heat.

steps.ttsScript: What is the sun? A huge star!
What does it give us? Light and heat!
You pulled two facts straight from the text. Nice reading!
Here is a helpful trick.
Put your finger on the exact words that answer.
Now the fact is easy to spot!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Now you read one! Here's a brand-new fact. Ants are tiny insects. They live together in a busy nest. Where do ants live?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! In a nest! You found that fact right in the text!
interactive.wrongScript: So close! Look back at the words. Where do the ants live? Try again!

steps.ttsScript: Your turn! Read each fact and find the answer.

lessons.title: Tricky Spellings
lessons.originalProblem: it's a grab-bag (silent letters + PH lumped together) and the tip is a study habit, not a transferable decoding skill

steps.ttsScript: Some words have a letter you write but never say.
We call it a silent letter. It hides in the word.
Let us learn how to find them.
In knee, the K is silent. We just say nee.
In lamb, the B is silent. We just say lam.
In wrist, the W is silent. We just say rist.
Silent letters love to hide at the start of a word.
Like the silent K in knot and the silent W in wrap.
They also hide at the end, like the silent B in climb.
Let's try one together. Here is a sneaky word.
Here is the word: comb.
Which letter is silent and hides? The B!
So do we say comb or come? We say come!
You skipped the silent B and read it right!
Here is a trick that always works.
If a word looks odd, try skipping the quiet letter and say it again.
Skip and say it. Now the word sounds right!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Your turn! Look at each word and find the letter that hides. Match each word to its silent letter.

interactive.prompt: Match each word to its silent letter
interactive.correctScript: You found them all! The G hides in sign, the K hides in knot, and the L hides in half!
interactive.wrongScript: Not quite. Say each word out loud and listen for the letter you never hear. Try again!

lessons.title: Using Smart Words
lessons.originalProblem: the proud/joyful/thrilled discrimination is too subtle for grade 2 and the 'correct' answer is debatable

steps.ttsScript: Words can show exactly how someone feels.
The right word paints a clear picture.
Different feelings have their own special words.
Scared means you feel afraid.
Curious means you really want to know.
Let's try one together. Here is a little story.
Sam yawned and could not keep his eyes open.
How does Sam feel? Tired!
The clue was the yawn. Tired fits best!
Here is a helpful trick.
Look for clues that show how someone feels.
The clue helps you pick the perfect word!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Now you try, word detective! Mia heard a loud noise in the dark and started to shake. Which word best shows how Mia feels?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! Scared! The loud noise in the dark made her shake. You picked the perfect word!
interactive.wrongScript: So close! Think about the clue. She heard a scary noise and started to shake. Try again!

lessons.title: Parts of Stories and Poems
lessons.originalProblem: It is pure term-labeling — the kid never sees a real stanza, scene, or chapter in context and never touches 'how each part builds on the one before,' which is the heart of RL.3.5

steps.ttsScript: Stories and poems are built from parts, like chapters and stanzas.
And each part builds on the one before it.
steps.displayText: Each part builds on the last

steps.ttsScript: A stanza is a group of lines in a poem, like a paragraph.
The first stanza sets things up. The next one moves the idea forward.
Let's try one together. Here is a short poem with two stanzas.
First stanza: The seed slept deep below the ground, waiting and warm, not making a sound.
steps.displayText: The seed slept deep below the ground, waiting and warm, not making a sound.

steps.ttsScript: What happens in stanza one? The seed waits underground!
Second stanza: Then up popped a leaf in the morning light, stretching up tall to the warm and bright.
steps.displayText: Then up popped a leaf in the morning light, stretching up tall.

steps.ttsScript: How does stanza two build on stanza one? The seed grows into a plant! Part two moves the story forward.
Here is a handy trick to remember.
At each new part, ask yourself: what changed from the part before?
That shows you how each part builds on the one before it.
steps.displayText: Each part builds on the last

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Now you try! Here is a poem. Stanza one: A storm rolled in, the sky turned gray, rain poured down all through the day. Stanza two: But morning came with golden sun, and out we ran to play and run. How does stanza two build on stanza one?

interactive.prompt: How does stanza two build on stanza one?
choices: The storm clears and the sun comes out
It describes the same rainy day again
interactive.correct: The storm clears and the sun comes out
interactive.correctScript: Yes! Stanza two builds on stanza one by showing the storm pass and the sun arrive. You followed how the parts connect!
interactive.wrongScript: So close! Reread stanza two. What changed from the gray storm to the morning? Try again!

steps.ttsScript: Your turn! Read each part and notice how it builds on the part before.

lessons.title: Connecting Events and Ideas
lessons.originalProblem: Standard is about connecting events/ideas (cause-effect, sequence, comparison) but the example only teaches cause-effect, then the Your Turn tests sequence ordering — a mismatch that leaves the modeled skill (cause-effect) untested and the tested skill (sequence) only briefly taught

steps.ttsScript: Events and ideas in nonfiction often connect.
Cause and effect. Sequence. Compare and contrast.
One thing makes another happen. The water spilled because the glass tipped.
Look for signal words like because, so, and as a result.
A cause makes an effect. The why and the what.
Sequence shows order. Compare and contrast shows same and different.
Let's try one together. Here's a true event.
The plant wilted because nobody watered it for a week.
steps.displayText: The plant wilted because nobody watered it.

steps.ttsScript: What signal word connects them? Because!
What caused the wilting? No water.
No water caused the plant to wilt. You connected cause and effect!
Here is a helpful trick.
Draw boxes and arrows to show how events connect.
Now you are ready to connect events and ideas!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Here's a new event: The sidewalk was icy, so Sam slipped and fell. What caused Sam to slip?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! The icy sidewalk caused Sam to slip. The word 'so' connected the cause and the effect!
interactive.wrongScript: Not quite! Look for the signal word 'so' in the sentence. What came right before it? Try again!

steps.ttsScript: Your turn to connect events and ideas on your own!
Watch for signal words and how events link.

lessons.title: Author's Point of View
lessons.originalProblem: The 'example' is an abstract three-step procedure (author's view / your view / compare) with no actual text to apply it to — it tells the strategy instead of modeling it on a real passage, weakening the bridge to the otherwise solid Your Turn

steps.ttsScript: Every author has a point of view.
You have your own view too. Notice when you agree or disagree.
Words like best, most important, or should signal an opinion.
Those words show the author's view, not yours!
Let's try one together. Here's a short passage.
Recess is the best part of the day. Kids need time to run and play outside.
steps.displayText: Recess is the best part of the day. Kids need time to run and play.

steps.ttsScript: What opinion word do you see? Best!
So how does the author feel about recess? They love it!
Here is a helpful trick.
Circle opinion words as you read. That is where the author shows their feeling.
Now you are ready to spot the author's view!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Listen closely. 'Everyone should visit the lake. Pack a lunch and stay all day. You will never want to leave!' How does the author feel about the lake?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! Loves it! Words like 'should' and 'never want to leave' show the author's view all on your own!
interactive.wrongScript: So close! Listen again - 'should visit' and 'never want to leave' are happy words. How does the author feel? Try again!

lessons.title: Reading Facts All Year
lessons.originalProblem: RI.3.10 is a range/stamina standard ('read and comprehend informational texts at the high end of the grade band') — it isn't a discrete skill, and the lesson papers over that by re-teaching main-idea/detail (RI.3.2) instead; also the correct answer 'Bats are amazing' is a vague title-feel answer that competes awkwardly with the more concrete distractors.

steps.ttsScript: This year you become a strong, all-year reader of fact books.
Good readers don't stop when a fact book gets long or tricky.
They keep going, page after page, until they finish the whole book.
Strong readers read about all kinds of subjects.
Space.Volcanoes.
Animals.Machines.
Let's try one together. Maya is reading a long fact book about sharks.
She gets to a hard page with a big new word she does not know.
steps.displayText: A hard page, a big new word

steps.ttsScript: Should Maya quit the book? No! She should keep reading.
What can help her keep going? Reread the tricky part slowly.
Maya kept going and finished her shark book. That's stamina!
When a fact book feels hard, use the stick-with-it trick!
Slow down and reread the part that confused you.
Then keep reading all the way to the last page.

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Now you try! Liam is reading a long book about deserts. He reaches a tricky page he doesn't understand. What should Liam do to be a strong all-year reader?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! Reread it and keep going. That's how a strong reader sticks with a hard book all year!
interactive.wrongScript: Not quite. Strong readers don't give up on a hard page. What helps you keep going? Try again!

lessons.title: Latin Suffixes
lessons.originalProblem: the 'from Latin' framing is decorative and never pays off; intro hook is hollow and the suffix set is a bit arbitrary

steps.ttsScript: A suffix is an ending we add to a word.
The ending gives us a clue to the word's meaning.
The suffix T-I-O-N turns an action into a thing.
steps.displayText: TION = an action becomes a thing

steps.ttsScript: Add it to act, and you get action. Add it to invent, and you get invention.
The suffix A-B-L-E means able to be done.
Break a word into its base and its ending. Wash plus able is washable.
Let's try decoding a word together. Here it is.
What is the base word? Break!
What is the suffix? Able!
So breakable means able to be broken. You decoded it!
Here is a trick for any long word.
Cover the suffix, read the base, then add the ending's meaning back.

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: You're a suffix detective now! Listen to this word: enjoyable. What does enjoyable mean?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! The base is enjoy and able means able to be done, so enjoyable means able to be enjoyed!
interactive.wrongScript: So close! Remember, the suffix able means able to be done. What is enjoy able to be? Try again!

steps.ttsScript: Your turn to be the detective!
Split each word, then find its meaning.

lessons.title: Using a Dictionary
lessons.originalProblem: No modeled example slide ('Let's Try One') — it tells about dictionaries but never models an actual lookup, and the 'Your Turn' (how are words organized?) is a trivial recall question, so the kid never practices the real skill of finding/reading an entry

steps.ttsScript: A dictionary tells you what a word means.
It also shows you how to say it.
Let's learn to look one up.
Words sit in alphabetical order.
Two guide words sit at the top of each page.
Your word fits between them.
Let's look up a word together. Here is the entry.
Here is the entry: gobble, gob-uhl, to eat something fast.
How do we say it? Gob-uhl!
What does it mean? To eat fast!
You read the whole entry. Nice work!
Here is a helpful trick.
An entry always goes word, then sound, then meaning.
Read it in that order every time!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Now you try! Here's a new entry: brittle, brit-uhl, easy to break. What does brittle mean?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! Easy to break! You read the meaning right from the entry!
interactive.wrongScript: Not yet! Look at the last part of the entry — what does it say it means? Try again!

lessons.title: Finding Story Details
lessons.originalProblem: the 'example' step only tells about inferring and never works through a passage, so the skill is quizzed without first being modeled

steps.ttsScript: Fourth grade readers use specific details from the text as evidence.
Sometimes the answer is right there. Sometimes you have to figure it out.
So, remember: good details prove your answer!
When you make a claim, point to the exact words from the text.
Other times the answer is hidden. You must infer it by putting clues together.
Both ways, the details are your proof.
Let's try one together. Here's a little story.
Sam tiptoed past the cake, then hid the gifts behind the couch and turned off all the lights.
steps.displayText: Sam hid the gifts behind the couch and turned off the lights.

steps.ttsScript: Where did Sam hide the gifts? Behind the couch! The text says it.
Why turn off the lights? It's a surprise party! We infer that from the clues.
One answer was stated, one we inferred. Nice detective work!
Here is a helpful trick.
When you answer, say: the words tell me... and name your clue!
Now you are ready to find story details!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Listen carefully to this short story. Lily pulled on her thickest sweater and wrapped a long scarf around her neck. She grabbed her mittens before heading out the door. What is the weather like outside?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! Cold! The sweater, scarf, and mittens were your clues. Great inferring!
interactive.wrongScript: So close! Think about Lily's sweater, scarf, and mittens. What weather needs those? Try again!

steps.ttsScript: Your turn! Let's find details and clues in new stories.

lessons.title: Poems, Drama, and Prose
lessons.originalProblem: No modeled example slide at all — it jumps from bare definitions straight to the kid's turn, so nothing demonstrates HOW to identify a form before they're asked to; poetry and prose are never shown, only drama.

steps.ttsScript: Stories come in three big forms.
These forms are poems,
drama, and prose.
Poems have lines, stanzas, and often rhythm or rhyme.
Drama is meant to be acted out. It uses scenes and dialogue.
Prose is regular sentences and paragraphs.
Let's try one together. Here is a short piece of writing.
The moon hangs high, a silver dime. It glows above the sea each night.
steps.displayText: The moon hangs high, a silver dime. / It glows above the sea each night.

steps.ttsScript: What clues do you see? It has short lines that rhyme!
So which form is it? A poem! Lines and rhyme give it away.
Here is a helpful trick.
Each form has its own clue word: stanza, scene, or paragraph.
Find the clue, and you find the form!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Now you try! Read this part. Scene One. Max walks in and says, Hello! Then Mia answers him. Which form is this?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! It's drama! The word Scene and the characters speaking show it's meant to be acted out.
interactive.wrongScript: Not quite. Look again. It says Scene One and the characters speak lines. Which form is acted out? Try again!

steps.ttsScript: Your turn! Let's practice spotting poems, drama, and prose.

lessons.title: Different Storytelling Voices
lessons.originalProblem: Skips the modeled example, so the kid sees definitions and then is immediately tested; it also conflates 'voice' with point of view loosely and never distinguishes third-limited vs third-omniscient, which RL.4.6 actually targets.

steps.ttsScript: Every story is told by a narrator. The narrator decides whose eyes we see through.
Some narrators say 'I'. Others say 'he' or 'she'. And some can even read minds!
When the narrator says 'he' or 'she' but only knows ONE character's thoughts, that is third-person limited.
It is like following one person around. You hear only what that person feels.
When the narrator knows what EVERY character is thinking, that is third-person omniscient.
Omniscient means all-knowing. This narrator floats above and sees inside everyone.
Let's try one together. Here is a short passage.
Maya gripped her bat, scared she might miss. Across the field, Leo hoped the ball would fly his way.
steps.displayText: Maya felt scared. Leo hoped the ball came his way.

steps.ttsScript: Does the narrator say I? No! It says Maya and Leo. So is it first or third person? Third!
Now, whose thoughts do we hear? We feel Maya's fear AND Leo's hope. Two minds!
Two minds means all-knowing. So this is third-person omniscient. You did it!
Here is a handy trick to remember.
Count the minds you can read. One mind is limited. Every mind is omniscient.

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Now you try, detective! Listen closely. 'Sam stared at the test, sure he would fail. Beside him, Priya secretly worried she had studied the wrong page.' Whose thoughts does the narrator share?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! You heard Sam's worry AND Priya's worry. Two minds means omniscient!
interactive.wrongScript: Think again. How many characters' thoughts did you hear in that passage? Try once more!

steps.ttsScript: You're ready! Time to practice spotting each narrator on your own.

lessons.title: Stories Across Mediums
lessons.originalProblem: Thin on the actual standard — RL.4.7 is about how a visual/oral presentation reflects specific text descriptions, but the lesson stays at a generic 'movies cut and add scenes' level and never models connecting a specific text moment to its visual realization.

steps.ttsScript: A story can be read as words, or watched as a movie.
Today we match a story's exact words to what we see on screen.
Authors give us exact details, like a green cloak with a silver clasp.
A good movie shows those very details on screen, not just any cloak.
Let's try one. Here is a line from a story.
The old lighthouse glowed red as waves crashed against the rocks.
steps.displayText: Lighthouse glowed red, waves crashed on rocks.

steps.ttsScript: Which detail must the movie show? A red glowing light!
And one more? Waves crashing on the rocks!
Here is a handy trick to remember.
Point to a detail in the words, then find that exact thing on screen.

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Your turn, director! Here is a sentence: The knight raised a golden shield as the dragon breathed orange fire. To match these exact words, what must the movie show on screen?

choices: A golden shield and orange fire
A castle on a tall hill
interactive.correct: A golden shield and orange fire
interactive.correctScript: Yes! A golden shield and orange fire. You matched the exact words to the screen!
interactive.wrongScript: Not quite. Look back at the exact details in the sentence. What could a camera actually show? Try again!

steps.ttsScript: Your turn! Let's match more story words to the screen.

lessons.title: Reading Big Stories
lessons.originalProblem: It teaches reading-stamina study skills, not comprehension of complex text — it sidesteps what the standard is actually about

steps.ttsScript: When a story gets longer, we read closely to understand it.
We watch the characters, the problem, and the clues.
Good readers ask who the story is about.
Then they ask what that person wants.
Watch for clues
that show how a hero feels
and what they do next.
Let's try one together. Here's part of a longer story.
Maya stared at the dark cave. Her hands shook, but she wanted to find her lost dog.
steps.displayText: Maya stared at the dark cave. Her hands shook, but she wanted to find her lost dog.

steps.ttsScript: How does Maya feel? Scared. Her shaking hands are the clue.
What does Maya want? To find her dog. That is why she keeps going.
Scared, but brave! You read the clues and understood Maya.
Here is a helpful trick.
Make a movie in your mind as you read each scene!
steps.displayText: Make a movie in your mind

steps.ttsScript: The clues become easy to see!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Here's a new story. Theo gripped the rope and looked up at the tall, steep cliff. He swallowed hard, but he wanted to reach the top first. How does Theo most likely feel as he looks up at the cliff?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! Nervous! Swallowing hard before a steep climb was your clue!
interactive.wrongScript: So close! Look at the clue, he swallowed hard before a tall, steep cliff. Try again!

lessons.title: Finding Fact Details
lessons.originalProblem: The inference half of the standard is asserted in a 3-word pill with no modeled example, and the Your Turn only tests literal recall

steps.ttsScript: Fourth grade nonfiction readers back up answers with text evidence.
Some answers are stated right in the words.
Other answers are hidden. You figure them out from clues.
Let's try one together. This answer is stated right in the words.
Bats sleep all day in dark caves. They hunt for insects at night.
steps.displayText: Bats sleep all day in dark caves. They hunt for insects at night.

steps.ttsScript: When do bats hunt? At night.
How do you know? The words say it right there. That's stated evidence.
You backed your answer with the words. That's how detectives read nonfiction!
Now a tricky one. This answer is hidden. We infer it from clues.
The desert sand burned Maya's feet. She gulped her whole water bottle fast.
steps.displayText: The desert sand burned Maya's feet. She gulped her whole water bottle fast.

steps.ttsScript: Was the desert hot or cold? Hot!
The story never says hot. Burning sand and gulping water are the clues.
You inferred it! The clues led you to a hidden answer. Nice detective work!
Here is a handy trick.
If the answer is hidden, ask: what do the clues prove?

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! The story never says it, so use the clues. Listen closely. Ben zipped up his thick coat and pulled his wool hat down low. His breath made little white clouds, and he stomped his boots to warm his toes. What season is it?

interactive.correctScript: Yes, winter! The thick coat, white breath, and cold toes were your clues. You inferred a hidden answer!
interactive.wrongScript: Not quite. The story never says the season, so use the clues. A thick coat and breath you can see mean it is very cold. Try again!

steps.ttsScript: Your turn! Find the stated answers and infer the hidden ones.

lessons.title: How Texts Are Built
lessons.originalProblem: the lesson teaches compare/contrast and problem/solution but the modeled example demonstrates sequence — a structure barely introduced — so the teaching and the model are misaligned

steps.ttsScript: Texts are organized in patterns.
One pattern compares and contrasts ideas.
Another pattern shows a problem and its solution.
A compare and contrast text
shows how things are alike
and how they are different.
A problem and solution text
names a trouble,
then shows how to fix it.
Let's try one together. Listen to this short passage.
Cats and dogs are both pets. But cats purr, while dogs bark.
steps.displayText: Cats and dogs are both pets. But cats purr, while dogs bark.

steps.ttsScript: How are they alike? Both are pets!
What text structure is it? Compare and contrast!
Alike and different words show it's compare and contrast. You spotted the structure!
Here is a helpful trick.
Words like both, but, and however signal compare and contrast.
Now you are ready to spot text structures!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Your turn, detective! Listen to this little story. A squirrel couldn't reach the nuts on the high branch. So, it found a long stick and used it to knock the nuts down. What text structure did I just use?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! Problem and solution! The squirrel had a trouble, then fixed it with a stick!
interactive.wrongScript: So close! Did the story show a trouble that got fixed? Try again!

lessons.title: Information Across Forms
lessons.originalProblem: the teaching stays abstract ('combine all information,' 'full picture') with no actual modeled example integrating two real sources, so the core RI.4.7 skill of synthesizing across forms is never demonstrated

steps.ttsScript: Information can come in text, charts, or diagrams.
When you put two forms together, you understand even more.
A chart shows the numbers.
Words explain the why behind those numbers.
Use both, and you get the whole story.
Let's try one together. Here are two sources about a school garden.
steps.displayText: Two sources: a chart and text

steps.ttsScript: The chart says: June, ten tomatoes. July, forty tomatoes.
The text says: In July, the class added water every day.
What does the chart show? More tomatoes in July!
Why did that happen? The text tells us: they watered every day. Combine both and you know the why!
Here is a helpful trick.
Let the chart tell you WHAT. Let the words tell you WHY.
Now you can pull the answer from both forms at once!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Now you try, researcher! A chart shows a town got way more rain in spring than in summer. A text says the town's flowers bloomed most in spring. Using BOTH sources, why did the flowers bloom most in spring?

interactive.prompt: Why did flowers bloom most in spring?
interactive.correctScript: Yes! You combined both sources! The chart showed the most rain in spring, and the text showed the most blooms in spring. That's synthesizing!
interactive.wrongScript: Not quite! Look at the chart and the text together. What did BOTH say happened most in spring? Try again!

steps.ttsScript: Your turn! Let's combine sources to find the full answer.

lessons.title: Author's Reasons and Evidence
lessons.originalProblem: no modeled example at all — it jumps from a thin teach on reasons/evidence straight to the kid's turn, so the link between a point, its reason, and its evidence is never shown in action

steps.ttsScript: Authors make a point. Then they back it up with reasons and evidence.
A reason answers one question: why?
It explains why the author's point is true.
Evidence is proof. Facts, examples, and numbers.
Let's try one together. Here is a short paragraph from an author.
Recess is important. Kids think better after they move. Studies show grades rise twenty percent.
steps.displayText: Recess is important. Kids think better after moving. Studies show grades rise twenty percent.

steps.ttsScript: What is the author's point? Recess is important!
What is the reason? Kids think better after they move!
What is the evidence? Grades rise twenty percent! That number is the proof.
Here is a handy trick.
Highlight reasons one color and evidence another. Watch how they link to the point!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Now you try, detective! Here's a new paragraph: Dogs make great pets. They keep you active. A vet counted that dog owners walk three miles every day. Which part is the evidence?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! 'Three miles a day' is a number, so it's the proof that backs up the point!
interactive.wrongScript: Close! Look for the part with a fact or number that proves the point. Try again!

steps.ttsScript: Your turn to hunt for reasons and evidence on your own!

lessons.title: Combining Two Texts
lessons.originalProblem: no worked example before the kid's turn — the integrate-two-texts skill is described abstractly in the teach/tip but never modeled, so the first time it's shown is the question itself

steps.ttsScript: When we read two texts on the same topic,
we get a stronger understanding.
Take a fact from the first text
and join it with a fact from the second.
Each text may cover a different angle.
Use both to see the whole picture.
Let's try one together. Here are two short texts about owls.
Text one says: Owls hunt at night. Text two says: Owls have huge eyes.
steps.displayText: 1: Owls hunt at night. 2: Owls have huge eyes.

steps.ttsScript: What does text one tell us? Owls hunt at night!
What does text two tell us? Owls have huge eyes!
Put them together: huge eyes help owls hunt in the dark! You combined both texts!
Here's a handy trick for joining two texts.
Ask: how do the facts connect?
The connection is your new, bigger idea.

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Now you try! One text says bees make sweet honey. Another text says bees carry pollen to flowers. Put both texts together. What do you understand better about bees?

interactive.correctScript: Yes! Why bees matter! Honey plus pollen shows bees help us and help flowers — you combined both texts!
interactive.wrongScript: Not quite. Put both facts together — sweet honey AND pollen for flowers. What bigger idea does that show? Try again!

steps.ttsScript: Your turn to combine two texts!
Find each fact, then join them.

lessons.title: Using Big Vocabulary
lessons.originalProblem: The intro/teach is thin and abstract ('use makes them yours', 'casual for chats') with only one concrete word total; a 4th grader gets little actual vocabulary or repeated modeling, so understanding stays shallow

steps.ttsScript: Big, exact words make your writing sound smart and clear.
Today we learn three: examine, enormous, and clever.
Examine means to look at something very closely.
Enormous means very, very big.
Clever means smart and quick at solving things.
Plain sentence: The dog is really big.
Better sentence: The dog is enormous!
Let's try one together. Here's a plain sentence to upgrade.
The sentence is: Maria looked at the bug.
Which big word means looked at closely? Examine!
So the upgraded sentence is: Maria examined the bug. Much stronger!
You swapped a plain word for a precise one. That's real vocabulary power!
Here is a helpful trick.
Learn one new word each day. Use it three times!
Soon those words will feel like your own!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Now you try! Match each big word to what it means.

interactive.prompt: Match each word to its meaning
interactive.correctScript: You matched them all! Examine is look closely, enormous is very big, and clever is smart and quick!
interactive.wrongScript: Not quite. Think about what each word really means, then try again!

lessons.title: Apostrophes and Commas
lessons.originalProblem: Commas (half the title) appear only in the tip slide with no teach or practice; lesson is lopsided toward apostrophes

steps.ttsScript: Two tiny marks do big jobs in sentences.
Apostrophes and commas.
Let us learn both!
An apostrophe replaces missing letters in a contraction.
Do not becomes don't. Can not becomes can't.
A comma separates each item when you name three or more things.
I packed socks, shoes, and a hat.
Let's try one together. Here's a sentence with a list.
Sam fed the dog the cat the fish. The marks are missing!
steps.displayText: Sam fed the dog the cat the fish

steps.ttsScript: How many things did Sam feed? Three animals!
What goes between them? A comma after each one!
So we write: Sam fed the dog, the cat, and the fish. Great work!
Here's a trick. A comma is a tiny pause.
Read your list out loud. Every spot you breathe needs a comma.
Now you are ready to use both marks!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Now you try! Here is a list with the marks missing: My garden grows beans corn and peas. Where do the commas belong?

interactive.prompt: Fix the list: beans corn and peas
interactive.correctScript: Yes! A comma after beans and after corn keeps every item clear!
interactive.wrongScript: So close! Put a comma between each thing in the list. Try again!

lessons.title: Punctuation Mastery
lessons.originalProblem: intro overpromises (periods, question marks, dialogue, titles) but only compound-sentence commas is actually taught and practiced; the quotation-mark half of the standard is mentioned once and never modeled or assessed

steps.ttsScript: Fourth graders master two big punctuation jobs.
First, commas that join two complete sentences.
Second, quotation marks that wrap what a character says out loud.
When two complete sentences join with and, but, or so, put a comma before that joining word.
Look: I packed my bag, and I caught the bus.
steps.displayText: I packed my bag, and I caught the bus.

steps.ttsScript: Both halves stand alone as sentences, so the comma sits right in front of and.
When a character speaks out loud, wrap their exact words in quotation marks.
Read this: Mia shouted, Wait for me!
A comma comes after shouted, and the end mark tucks inside the closing quote.
Let's try one together. Here is a line where someone speaks.
Here is the line: Sam grinned and whispered, I found the treasure.
steps.displayText: Sam grinned and whispered, “I found the treasure.”

steps.ttsScript: What marks should wrap the words Sam speaks out loud? Quotation marks!
Where does the period belong? Inside! It tucks right inside the closing quote.
So we write: Sam whispered, open-quote I found the treasure period close-quote. You nailed it!
Here is a quick trick for both marks.
Ask: is someone speaking? Use quotes. Are two sentences joined? Use a comma.
Two questions, two marks. Now you are ready!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Your turn! Punctuation has two big jobs. Match each writing situation to the mark it needs.

interactive.prompt: Match each situation to its mark
interactive.correctScript: You matched them all! Spoken words get quotes, joined sentences get a comma, and the period tucks inside.
interactive.wrongScript: Not quite. Think about each job: who is speaking, and where do sentences join? Try again!

lessons.title: Storytime All Year
lessons.originalProblem: the Your Turn distractors (close your eyes, skip the pages) are too obviously wrong, so it tests almost no real understanding

steps.ttsScript: Look! Reading stories every day is so much fun.
Each story takes you on a new adventure.
Let us learn how to be a great reading helper.
When we read together, you can join in!
Listen closely and look at the pictures.
Pictures help you know what is happening.
A good reader asks questions about the story.
You can answer questions too.
Sharing your ideas helps everyone understand.
Let's try one together! We are all reading a story.
The teacher asks: Where did the bear go?
What is a good way to help? Raise your hand and answer!
You said the bear went to the cave. Great job joining in!
Here is a tip to remember.
Eyes open, ears ready, hand up to share!

slides.heading: Your Turn!
slides.spokenQ: Now you try! Your class is reading a story about a lost puppy. The teacher asks, why is the puppy sad? What is the best way to help with the story?

interactive.prompt: What is the best way to help?
choices: Wait for someone else to talk
interactive.correctScript: Yes! Raising your hand to answer helps everyone understand the story together!
interactive.wrongScript: Good thinking! But the best helper joins in. What could you do when the teacher asks a question? Try again!

steps.ttsScript: Your turn! Let's practice being a great reading helper.
Remember to listen, look, and share!
